source: CARDI book "ដំណាំស្រូវនៅកម្ពុជា" (Rice Cultivation in Cambodia), by Men Sarom, Thuy Lina and Pheng Thimuny, published by CARDI, 2007, Chapter 2 (Rice-growing environment), by Preap Visarto, section 2.3 (Light). No elibrary URL visible.
text: Sunlight affects rice growth through both day length (photoperiod) and light intensity/quality. Day length: rice varieties differ in photoperiod sensitivity - photoperiod-sensitive varieties only begin flowering once day length shortens below a critical threshold (roughly 10-11 hours in this region), meaning they flower at a fixed time of year regardless of planting date, while photoperiod-insensitive varieties flower at a fixed number of days after planting/emergence regardless of day length (citing Men Sarom's own 1996 barley research on developmental variation, applied here by analogy to rice). This distinction matters for matching variety choice to planting schedule flexibility. Light intensity: photosynthesis rate rises with light intensity up to a saturation point, and reduced light (e.g. during a cloudy/rainy period) lowers photosynthesis and can reduce yield, especially if it occurs during the grain-filling period - the source notes yield can drop by roughly 60% if shading is severe and sustained during this critical window, since this is when the plant most needs stored carbohydrate reserves built during earlier photosynthesis. Light quality: different wavelengths affect the plant differently - blue light (around 4000 Angstroms) is described as favoring vegetative growth, while red light (roughly 5600-7200 Angstroms) favors reproductive-stage processes; infrared and ultraviolet wavelengths were noted as having comparatively minor direct growth effects.
caveat: This is foundational crop-physiology/environment content, useful as background for understanding variety choice (photoperiod-sensitive vs. insensitive) and the importance of avoiding heavy shading during grain-fill. Recommend a duplicate-check against any existing cropping-calendar or variety-classification content once repo access is available.
